lessons.title: AMH in PCOS diagnosis
lessons.objective: Know when AMH can replace ultrasound to define polycystic ovarian morphology and when it adds nothing.
lessons.closing: AMH entered PCOS diagnosis only as an alternative to ultrasound in adults, never as a single test and not in adolescents.

lessons.title: Glycaemia and insulin in PCOS
lessons.objective: Order the right glycaemic assessment in PCOS and avoid insulin tests with no clinical value.
lessons.closing: Assess glycaemia in everyone, with a 75 g OGTT as the most accurate test; do not measure insulin routinely even though insulin resistance is part of the mechanism.

lessons.title: Inositol, metformin, diet and letrozole
lessons.objective: Place each option according to recommendation strength and evidence certainty, without false equivalence.
lessons.closing: For ovulation induction, letrozole has the firmest recommendation. Metformin and inositol are conditional: very low certainty for metabolic outcomes; in infertility, metformin has low certainty and inositol is considered experimental. No specific diet beats another.

items.title: AMH as an alternative to ultrasound in adults
items.core: In adults, serum AMH could be used to define polycystic ovarian morphology (conditional recommendation, moderate certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
PCOS diagnosis in adults requires two of three elements (ovulatory dysfunction, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries), after excluding other causes. The 2023 guideline lets AMH replace ultrasound for that third element. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

AMH or ultrasound, but not both: ordering both increases the risk of overdiagnosis (practice point 1.5.5). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: In which patients, and for which criterion, can AMH be used in PCOS diagnosis?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: International PCOS guideline 2023: conditional, moderate certainty.

items.title: When AMH adds nothing in PCOS
items.core: AMH should not be used as a single test to diagnose PCOS, nor, for now, in adolescents (both strong recommendations). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
If a patient already has irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism, she meets criteria: AMH is not needed for diagnosis (strong recommendation). In adolescents there are no definitive ultrasound criteria for polycystic ovarian morphology, and AMH is not recommended either. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

In addition, AMH may be suppressed by current or recent combined hormonal contraception (the guideline also lists ovarian surgery among the factors to consider), varies with age, BMI and cycle day, and must be read against assay-specific cut-offs (practice points 1.5.6 and 1.5.7). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: In which situations should you not order AMH to diagnose PCOS, and what can alter it?
items.pearl: Before ordering AMH for suspected PCOS, ask yourself which criterion is missing and whether she uses combined contraception. If none is missing, don’t order it.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: International PCOS guideline 2023: strong recommendations, moderate certainty.

items.title: Assess glycaemia in everyone at diagnosis
items.core: Glycaemic status should be assessed at diagnosis in all adults and adolescents with PCOS (strong recommendation). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
The guideline notes that, regardless of age and BMI, women with PCOS have an increased risk of impaired fasting glucose, impaired glucose tolerance and type 2 diabetes. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

The 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is the most accurate test, regardless of BMI (strong, very low certainty); if it cannot be done, fasting glucose and/or HbA1c could be considered, being less accurate (conditional). Reassess every 1–3 years based on risk factors (consensus). In fertility: consider an OGTT when planning pregnancy or fertility treatment (conditional, very low certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: Who gets glycaemic assessment in PCOS, and with which test?

rows.text: If not possible: fasting glucose and/or HbA1c (less accurate)

visual.alt: Flow: in any diagnosed PCOS, whatever the BMI, the 75 g OGTT is the most accurate test; if not possible, fasting glucose and/or HbA1c, which are less accurate.

items.application: Don’t limit glycaemic assessment to patients with overweight: the recommendation covers any BMI. If she plans pregnancy or fertility treatment, that is the time for an OGTT.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Strong; low to very low certainty depending on the recommendation.

items.title: What I would not order: routine insulin or HOMA
items.core: Insulin resistance is a pathophysiological factor in PCOS, but clinically available insulin assays are of limited clinical relevance and should not be used in routine care. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
It is a practice point in the 2023 guideline (expert consensus, no certainty rating). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

The mechanism is real, but measuring it does not change management: what guides care is glycaemic assessment and cardiometabolic risk. Ordering insulin or calculating HOMA “to confirm” resistance adds cost and confusion without changing the plan.
items.recall: Why is routine insulin measurement not recommended in PCOS if insulin resistance is part of the mechanism?
items.pearl: A true mechanism does not make a useful test.

items.title: Inositol in PCOS: conditional option, mixed evidence
items.core: Inositol, in any form, could be considered based on preferences and values, noting limited harm, potential improvement in metabolic measures and limited clinical benefit, including in ovulation, hirsutism or weight (conditional, very low certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
In women with PCOS and infertility, inositol alone or combined should be considered experimental therapy (conditional, very low certainty); in that context the guideline states that its side effects and safety are not known. For hirsutism and central adiposity metformin is preferred, though it has more gastrointestinal side effects. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

The systematic review that informed the guideline found mixed evidence from small, heterogeneous trials. [[ref:fitz-2024-inositol-pcos]] The guideline does not recommend specific types, doses or combinations, and product quality and regulation vary. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.recall: What does the 2023 guideline say about inositol, and what does it not specify?
items.application: If a patient wants to use it, it is a shared decision: explain the very low certainty, that it is experimental in infertility and that product quality varies; ask her to tell her clinicians.

evidence.label: limited
evidence.note: Conditional, very low certainty; experimental in infertility; no recommended dose.

items.title: Metformin: by BMI and by goal
items.core: In adults with PCOS and BMI ≥25 kg/m², metformin alone should be considered for anthropometric and metabolic outcomes (insulin resistance, glucose and lipids) (conditional, very low certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
With BMI <25 kg/m², it may be considered, acknowledging limited evidence (consensus recommendation). In anovulatory infertility with no other factors, metformin alone could be used to improve clinical pregnancy and live birth, informing that more effective ovulation induction agents exist (conditional, low certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

Note the verbs: “should be considered”, “may be considered”, “could be used”. All are conditional; none is a universal indication.
items.recall: How does the metformin recommendation change with BMI and with the goal (metabolic or fertility)?
items.application: In Spain, the Dianben (metformin) product information covers only type 2 diabetes: its use in PCOS is off-label. [[ref:aemps-2025-dianben-ft]]

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Conditional (metabolic: very low certainty; fertility: low) and consensus (BMI <25).

items.title: There is no “PCOS diet”
items.core: There is no evidence to support one diet composition over another in PCOS (conditional, very low certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
Any eating pattern consistent with population healthy-eating guidelines will have health benefits (consensus recommendation, strong). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

In practice (interpretation, not a guideline recommendation): choose the pattern the patient can sustain, without unnecessary restrictions.
items.recall: Is there a preferred diet composition for PCOS according to the 2023 guideline?
items.application: Faced with “do I have to cut gluten or dairy because of PCOS?”: the guideline does not support any specific composition.

items.title: Letrozole: first line for ovulation induction
items.core: Letrozole should be the first-line pharmacological treatment for ovulation induction in infertile anovulatory women with PCOS and no other infertility factors (strong recommendation, high certainty). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]
items.body:
It is one of the highest-certainty recommendations in the guideline, which also prefers letrozole over clomiphene in this setting. Its use is still off-label in many countries, which should be explained to patients. [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]]

It should not be given where there is any possibility of a pre-existing pregnancy, although there is no evidence of greater teratogenicity than with other induction agents (practice point 5.3.3). [[ref:teede-2023-pcos-guideline]] By contrast, metformin alone in infertility is conditional with low certainty, and inositol is considered experimental.
items.recall: Which drug is first line for ovulation induction in PCOS, and with what strength and certainty?
items.application: In Spain, the Femara product information (reference letrozole) lists only breast cancer indications, so its use for ovulation induction is off-label. Clomiphene (Omifin) is licensed for anovulatory or dysovulatory infertility, including PCOS. [[ref:aemps-2025-femara-ft]] [[ref:aemps-2021-omifin-ft]]

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman with 45–60-day cycles and clinical hirsutism. Is an AMH needed to diagnose PCOS?

options.text: Yes, AMH confirms the diagnosis.
options.why: AMH should not be used as a single test for PCOS.

options.text: No: with irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism she already meets criteria; AMH is not needed.
options.why: Correct: strong recommendation in the 2023 guideline (after excluding other causes).

options.text: Yes, plus an ultrasound to count follicles.
options.why: No criterion is missing: neither AMH nor ultrasound is needed for diagnosis.

options.text: Only if BMI is ≥25 kg/m².
options.why: BMI does not change the diagnostic criteria.

items.explanation: Before ordering AMH, ask yourself which criterion is missing. Diagnosis also requires excluding other causes.

items.stem: According to the 2023 guideline, in which patient could AMH be used to define polycystic ovarian morphology?

options.text: A 15-year-old with irregular cycles.
options.why: AMH should not yet be used in adolescents.

options.text: An adult with hyperandrogenism and regular cycles who is missing one criterion.
options.why: Correct: in adults, AMH can replace ultrasound for that criterion.

options.text: Any woman, as a single PCOS test.
options.why: It should not be used as a single test.

options.text: An adult with irregular cycles and hyperandrogenism.
options.why: She already meets criteria: AMH is not needed.

items.explanation: AMH helps in adults when the morphology criterion is missing, never as a single test and not in adolescents.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with newly diagnosed PCOS and BMI 21 kg/m². Which glycaemic assessment is appropriate?

options.text: None, because her weight is normal.
options.why: Glycaemic assessment is recommended for everyone, whatever the BMI.

options.text: Fasting insulin and HOMA.
options.why: Insulin assays should not be used in routine care.

options.text: A 75 g OGTT, the most accurate test.
options.why: Correct: strong recommendation, regardless of BMI.

options.text: HbA1c only, because it is the most accurate.
options.why: HbA1c is a less accurate alternative if an OGTT is not possible.

items.explanation: Everyone, at diagnosis, with a 75 g OGTT as the preferred test.

items.stem: A patient with PCOS brings a high HOMA-IR from a private lab and asks whether it confirms her diagnosis. What is most accurate?

options.text: It confirms PCOS.
options.why: Insulin resistance is not a diagnostic criterion for PCOS.

options.text: It means she must start metformin.
options.why: The metformin decision is not based on an insulin assay, and the recommendation is conditional.

options.text: Insulin resistance is part of the mechanism, but these measurements have limited clinical value; glycaemic assessment is what helps.
options.why: Correct: a practice point in the 2023 guideline.

options.text: It should be repeated every 3 months to monitor treatment.
options.why: They are not recommended routinely; repeating them does not improve care.

items.explanation: A true mechanism does not make a useful test.

items.stem: Which statement about inositol in PCOS is consistent with the 2023 guideline?

options.text: Myo-inositol at a standard dose is recommended for everyone.
options.why: The guideline does not recommend specific types, doses or combinations.

options.text: It could be considered based on preferences and values, with very low certainty.
options.why: Correct: conditional recommendation, very low certainty.

options.text: Its safety is well established, so there is no need to report it.
options.why: Side effects and safety are not well known; patients are encouraged to tell their clinicians.

options.text: It has the same recommendation strength as letrozole for ovulation.
options.why: Letrozole: strong, high certainty; inositol: conditional, very low certainty.

items.explanation: Shared decision, no recommended dose and variable product quality.

items.stem: A patient with PCOS asks which specific diet she should follow. Which answer reflects the 2023 guideline?

options.text: A ketogenic diet, because it is the most effective in PCOS.
options.why: There is no evidence that one composition beats another.

options.text: Gluten-free and dairy-free for everyone.
options.why: The guideline does not support specific exclusions.

options.text: No composition has proven superior; a healthy, sustainable pattern has benefits.
options.why: Correct: consistent with the 2023 recommendations.

options.text: Mandatory intermittent fasting.
options.why: There is no evidence of superiority for any specific strategy.

items.explanation: Whatever the patient can sustain, consistent with healthy-eating guidelines.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with PCOS, anovulatory, trying to conceive; partner with normal semen analysis and patent tubes. First-line pharmacological ovulation induction?

options.text: Letrozole.
options.why: Correct: strong recommendation with high certainty.

options.text: Inositol.
options.why: In infertility, inositol is considered experimental therapy; it is not first line.

options.text: Straight to IVF.
options.why: Without other factors, first line is ovulation induction with letrozole.

options.text: Metformin alone as first line for ovulation.
options.why: Metformin alone could be used (conditional, low certainty), but more effective agents exist: first line is letrozole.

items.explanation: Letrozole is first line in anovulatory women with PCOS and no other factors; in many countries it is used off-label.

items.stem: Which pair is correctly graded according to the 2023 guideline?

options.text: Metformin with BMI ≥25 (metabolic outcomes): conditional, very low certainty.
options.why: Correct.

options.text: Metformin with BMI <25: strong, high certainty.
options.why: With BMI <25 it is a consensus recommendation acknowledging limited evidence.

options.text: Inositol: strong, moderate certainty.
options.why: Inositol: conditional, very low certainty.

options.text: Letrozole for ovulation: conditional, low certainty.
options.why: Letrozole: strong, high certainty.

items.explanation: Knowing each option's strength and certainty avoids false equivalence between treatments.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman with regular cycles and biochemical hyperandrogenism already has an ultrasound showing polycystic ovarian morphology (PCOM). What does also ordering a serum AMH add?

options.text: It is mandatory to confirm the ultrasound finding before diagnosis.
options.why: The 2023 guideline allows AMH or ultrasound to define PCOM; it does not require both.

options.text: It serves to exclude other causes of hyperandrogenism.
options.why: AMH can only be used to define PCOM; it is not the test for excluding other causes.

options.text: Nothing useful: AMH or ultrasound, but not both, because ordering both increases the risk of overdiagnosis.
options.why: Correct: practice point 1.5.5 of the 2023 international PCOS guideline.

options.text: It allows hyperandrogenism to be dropped as a criterion.
options.why: AMH can only take the place of the polycystic ovary criterion; it does not replace other criteria.

items.explanation: With hyperandrogenism and PCOM on ultrasound there are already two of three elements; a second morphology test only adds overdiagnosis risk. Diagnosis also requires excluding other causes.

items.stem: According to the 2023 international PCOS guideline, with what strength and certainty can serum AMH be used to define polycystic ovarian morphology in adults?

options.text: Strong recommendation, high certainty.
options.why: It is neither strong nor high certainty: it is conditional with moderate certainty.

options.text: Strong recommendation, moderate certainty.
options.why: The limits are strong (not as a single test, not in adolescents); use to define PCOM is conditional.

options.text: Practice point, with no certainty rating.
options.why: The practice point is the advice not to order AMH and ultrasound together (1.5.5), not the use of AMH to define PCOM.

options.text: Conditional recommendation, moderate certainty.
options.why: Correct: recommendation 1.5.1 of the 2023 guideline (“could be used”).

items.explanation: Conditional (“could be used”) to define PCOM in adults; by contrast, not using it as a single test or in adolescents are strong recommendations.

items.stem: A 26-year-old woman with irregular cycles and no hyperandrogenism, who used combined hormonal contraception until two months ago. Her AMH is normal. How do you interpret it according to the 2023 guideline?

options.text: It rules out PCOS: with a normal AMH there is no polycystic ovarian morphology.
options.why: AMH is not a single test for PCOS, and recent combined contraception may suppress it.

options.text: With caution: current or recent combined contraceptive use may suppress AMH.
options.why: Correct: practice point 1.5.6 (factors influencing AMH).

options.text: Contraception does not affect AMH, so the result is reliable.
options.why: The guideline notes that current or recent combined contraception may suppress AMH.

options.text: It is enough to compare it with a universal cut-off valid for any laboratory.
options.why: The guideline asks for population- and assay-specific cut-offs (1.5.7).

items.explanation: Before interpreting an AMH, ask about current or recent combined contraception and use population- and assay-specific cut-offs.

items.stem: Which of these statements about factors that influence AMH is correct according to the practice points of the 2023 PCOS guideline?

options.text: In the general population, serum AMH is lower with a higher BMI.
options.why: Correct: practice point 1.5.6, which also lists age, contraception, ovarian surgery and cycle day.

options.text: AMH is stable across the menstrual cycle, so the sampling day does not matter.
options.why: The guideline notes that AMH may vary across the cycle.

options.text: Combined hormonal contraception raises AMH.
options.why: It is the opposite: it may suppress it.

options.text: A single cut-off common to all assays can be used.
options.why: The guideline asks for population- and assay-specific cut-offs.

items.explanation: The guideline asks to take into account age, BMI, combined contraception (under a heading that also names ovarian surgery) and cycle day; that is why AMH is read against population- and assay-specific cut-offs.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman with PCOS, BMI 23 kg/m², planning fertility treatment next year. Two years ago her fasting glucose was normal. What is most consistent with the 2023 guideline?

options.text: No test: normal BMI and previous normal glucose.
options.why: Glycaemic assessment does not depend on BMI, and planning pregnancy or fertility treatment is the moment to consider an OGTT.

options.text: HbA1c only, as it is more accurate than an OGTT.
options.why: It is the opposite: the 75 g OGTT is the most accurate test; HbA1c is less accurate.

options.text: Consider a 75 g OGTT when planning pregnancy or fertility treatment.
options.why: Correct: conditional recommendation of the 2023 guideline (very low certainty), whatever the BMI.

options.text: Fasting insulin and HOMA to decide whether an OGTT is needed.
options.why: The guideline does not recommend insulin assays in routine care.

items.explanation: Normal weight is not the same as normal glycaemia in PCOS. Before trying to conceive or fertility treatment, the guideline proposes considering an OGTT.

items.stem: In PCOS, if a 75 g OGTT cannot be done, what does the 2023 guideline propose, and how often should glycaemic status be reassessed?

options.text: HbA1c, as accurate as the OGTT; reassess only if BMI increases.
options.why: HbA1c is less accurate, and reassessment is based on risk factors, not just BMI.

options.text: Fasting glucose and/or HbA1c, less accurate; reassess every 1–3 years based on risk factors.
options.why: Correct: conditional alternative if no OGTT, and consensus reassessment every 1–3 years.

options.text: Fasting insulin; reassess every year.
options.why: Insulin assays are not used in routine care.

options.text: No alternative; assess only once at diagnosis.
options.why: There is an alternative (fasting glucose and/or HbA1c) and reassessment is periodic.

items.explanation: Glycaemic assessment for everyone at diagnosis; OGTT as the most accurate test; if not possible, fasting glucose and/or HbA1c; reassess every 1–3 years based on risk.

items.stem: A resident proposes ordering fasting insulin in all patients with PCOS and doing an OGTT only in those with insulin resistance. What does the 2023 guideline answer?

options.text: It is reasonable: only insulin-resistant patients need glycaemic assessment.
options.why: Glycaemic assessment is recommended for everyone, whatever the BMI.

options.text: Better to calculate HOMA than to order fasting insulin.
options.why: HOMA relies on the same insulin measurement and shares its limited clinical value.

options.text: Only in patients with BMI ≥25 kg/m².
options.why: BMI does not change the indication: no routine insulin and no restricted glycaemic assessment.

options.text: No: insulin assays are of limited clinical relevance and not used routinely; glycaemic assessment is for everyone.
options.why: Correct: 2023 guideline practice point and strong recommendation to assess glycaemia in everyone.

items.explanation: Insulin levels are not a useful filter: the guideline asks to assess glycaemia in everyone, with the 75 g OGTT as the most accurate test.

items.stem: In the 2023 PCOS guideline, what type of statement indicates that available insulin assays should not be used in routine care?

options.text: A practice point (expert consensus), with no certainty rating.
options.why: Correct: practice points 1.9.12 and 3.1.10.

options.text: An evidence-based recommendation, strong and high certainty.
options.why: It is not an evidence-based recommendation but a practice point.

options.text: A conditional recommendation of very low certainty.
options.why: It carries no certainty rating: it is a practice point.

options.text: The guideline says nothing about insulin assays.
options.why: It does, in two practice points.

items.explanation: Being consensus does not make it optional: the guideline recognises insulin resistance as a mechanism, but not its routine measurement.

items.stem: A woman with PCOS and anovulatory infertility, no other factors, asks whether she can use inositol instead of medication to ovulate. What does the 2023 guideline say?

options.text: It is first line because of its good safety profile.
options.why: First-line pharmacological treatment is letrozole; in infertility the guideline says inositol safety is not known.

options.text: It can be used with the type, dose and combination the guideline recommends.
options.why: The guideline does not recommend specific types, doses or combinations.

options.text: In infertility, inositol alone or combined should be considered experimental therapy.
options.why: Correct: conditional recommendation, very low certainty; side effects and safety not known.

options.text: It is equivalent to letrozole for live birth rate.
options.why: There is no basis for that equivalence: letrozole is first line with high certainty and inositol is experimental.

items.explanation: In fertility, the guideline draws a clear line: letrozole first line (strong, high certainty); inositol experimental.

items.stem: For hirsutism and central adiposity in PCOS, what does the 2023 guideline say when comparing metformin and inositol?

options.text: Inositol is preferred because it has fewer gastrointestinal effects.
options.why: Fewer gastrointestinal effects do not make it preferable: the guideline prefers metformin for these outcomes.

options.text: Metformin should be considered over inositol, noting that metformin has more gastrointestinal side effects.
options.why: Correct: conditional recommendation of the 2023 guideline.

options.text: They are equivalent; either may be chosen.
options.why: The guideline does not consider them equivalent for these outcomes.

options.text: Neither has a place in PCOS.
options.why: Both have conditional recommendations in the guideline.

items.explanation: If she uses inositol, make it a shared decision, knowing that product quality varies, and ask her to tell her clinicians.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman with PCOS, BMI 22 kg/m², not trying to conceive, asks about metformin “to improve her metabolism”. What does the 2023 guideline say?

options.text: It should be considered under the same evidence-based recommendation as with BMI ≥25 kg/m².
options.why: That recommendation is for BMI ≥25; with BMI <25 it is a consensus that acknowledges limited evidence.

options.text: It is contraindicated with BMI <25 kg/m².
options.why: There is no such contraindication: the guideline says it may be considered.

options.text: It is a universal indication in all PCOS.
options.why: All metformin recommendations are conditional or consensus; none is universal.

options.text: It may be considered, acknowledging limited evidence.
options.why: Correct: consensus recommendation for BMI <25 kg/m².

items.explanation: Note the verbs: “should be considered” (BMI ≥25), “may be considered” (BMI <25), “could be used” (infertility). None is a universal indication.

items.stem: In Spain, what does the Dianben (metformin) product information state regarding PCOS?

options.text: Its indications are limited to type 2 diabetes: use in PCOS is off-label.
options.why: Correct: section 4.1 lists only type 2 diabetes mellitus.

options.text: It includes PCOS with BMI ≥25 kg/m².
options.why: That threshold comes from the international guideline, not from the product information.

options.text: It includes anovulatory infertility.
options.why: The product information lists no fertility indications.

options.text: It includes PCOS in adolescents from age 10.
options.why: Use from age 10 refers to type 2 diabetes, not PCOS.

items.explanation: The international guideline and the product information answer different questions: what is reasonable per the evidence and what is licensed. In Spain, metformin in PCOS is off-label use.

items.stem: In the 2023 PCOS guideline, how are the two statements on diet graded?

options.text: Both are strong evidence-based recommendations with high certainty.
options.why: Neither has high certainty: one is conditional with very low certainty and the other is consensus.

options.text: “No composition is superior”: practice point; “healthy pattern”: conditional.
options.why: Neither is a practice point: the composition statement is conditional with very low certainty, and the healthy-pattern statement is consensus and strong.

options.text: “No composition is superior”: conditional, very low certainty; “any healthy pattern consistent with population guidelines”: consensus, strong.
options.why: Correct: recommendations 3.3.1 and 3.3.2.

options.text: The guideline does not grade its diet recommendations.
options.why: It does grade them: 3.3.1 and 3.3.2.

items.explanation: Very low certainty about composition does not mean eating well is irrelevant: the strong consensus supports a healthy, sustainable pattern.

items.stem: A patient with PCOS already follows a varied, healthy eating pattern that she sustains without difficulty. She has read that a “PCOS-specific low-glycaemic-index diet” is better and asks whether she should switch. What is consistent with the 2023 guideline?

options.text: Switch, because the guideline recommends a low-glycaemic-index diet in PCOS.
options.why: The guideline finds no evidence that one composition beats another.

options.text: Switch only if she wants better hormonal outcomes, where that diet is superior.
options.why: There is no evidence of superiority for hormonal outcomes either.

options.text: No need to switch because of PCOS: no composition has been shown to be superior, and a healthy pattern she can sustain already has benefits.
options.why: Correct: recommendations 3.3.1 (conditional, very low certainty) and 3.3.2 (consensus, strong).

options.text: Keep her pattern but add restrictions to strengthen the effect.
options.why: The guideline asks to avoid unduly restrictive or unbalanced diets (3.3.3).

items.explanation: If the pattern is healthy and sustainable, changing it “because of PCOS” has no support; any change should be tailored to her preferences and goals.

items.stem: Which caution does the 2023 PCOS guideline give when prescribing letrozole for ovulation induction?

options.text: That it is more teratogenic than clomiphene.
options.why: The guideline says there is no evidence of greater teratogenicity than with other induction agents.

options.text: That it can only be used after clomiphene fails.
options.why: It is first line, and the guideline prefers it over clomiphene.

options.text: That it must always be combined with metformin.
options.why: The guideline does not require that combination.

options.text: That it should not be given if there is any possibility of a pre-existing pregnancy, though there is no evidence of more teratogenicity than with other agents.
options.why: Correct: practice point 5.3.3.

items.explanation: Rule out pregnancy before each letrozole cycle; the caution is not based on proven greater teratogenicity.

items.stem: The 2023 international PCOS guideline recommends letrozole as first line for ovulation induction. In Spain, what do the product information documents for letrozole (Femara) and clomiphene (Omifin) state?

options.text: Femara has only breast cancer indications (ovulation induction off-label); Omifin is licensed for anovulatory or dysovulatory infertility, including PCOS.
options.why: Correct: section 4.1 of both product information documents.

options.text: Both are licensed for ovulation induction in PCOS.
options.why: Femara lists only breast cancer indications.

options.text: Letrozole is licensed for PCOS and clomiphene is not.
options.why: It is the other way round.

options.text: Neither is licensed, so the guideline does not apply in Spain.
options.why: Omifin is licensed; and off-label use does not invalidate the recommendation: where allowed, it requires informing the patient and discussing the evidence.

items.explanation: The guideline recommends letrozole; the Spanish product information does not license it for that indication. The guideline itself notes it is off-label in many countries: where allowed, inform the patient and discuss the evidence; where not, other induction agents can be used.

aemps-2021-omifin-ft.title: Ficha técnica de Omifin 50 mg comprimidos (citrato de clomifeno)
aemps-2021-omifin-ft.population: Women with anovulatory or dysovulatory infertility (Spain).
aemps-2021-omifin-ft.finding: Indicated for normoprolactinaemic functional anovulatory or dysovulatory infertility (including luteal insufficiency and polycystic ovary syndrome), as a test in certain amenorrhoeas, and for ovulation induction in assisted reproduction (intrauterine insemination, IVF).
aemps-2021-omifin-ft.limitations: Only section 4.1 was read (SmPC dated 4 December 2021). It is the only clomiphene listed in CIMA.

aemps-2025-dianben-ft.title: Ficha técnica de Dianben 850 mg comprimidos recubiertos con película (metformina)
aemps-2025-dianben-ft.population: Adults and children from 10 years with type 2 diabetes (Spain).
aemps-2025-dianben-ft.finding: Only indication: type 2 diabetes when diet and exercise are insufficient, alone or in combination; PCOS is not mentioned.
aemps-2025-dianben-ft.limitations: Only section 4.1 of one brand was read (SmPC dated 5 May 2025).

aemps-2025-femara-ft.title: Ficha técnica de Femara 2,5 mg comprimidos recubiertos con película (letrozol)
aemps-2025-femara-ft.population: Postmenopausal women with hormone-dependent breast cancer (Spain).
aemps-2025-femara-ft.finding: All indications are for breast cancer (adjuvant, extended adjuvant, advanced and neoadjuvant); there is no ovulation induction indication.
aemps-2025-femara-ft.limitations: Only section 4.1 of the reference brand was read (SmPC dated 14 April 2025); CIMA lists 41 letrozole presentations whose SmPCs were not read.

fitz-2024-inositol-pcos.title: Inositol for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis to Inform the 2023 Update of the International Evidence-based PCOS Guidelines
fitz-2024-inositol-pcos.authors: Fitz V, Graca S, Mahalingaiah S, et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2024;109(6):1630-1655
fitz-2024-inositol-pcos.population: 30 trials (n=2230) in adolescents and adults with PCOS; 19 meta-analysed.
fitz-2024-inositol-pcos.finding: Mixed evidence: possible benefits of myo-inositol or D-chiro-inositol on some metabolic measures and a possible benefit of D-chiro-inositol on ovulation; no effect on other outcomes.
fitz-2024-inositol-pcos.limitations: Only the abstract was verified; small, heterogeneous trials (inositol type, dose and combinations).

teede-2023-pcos-guideline.title: Recommendations From the 2023 International Evidence-based Guideline for the Assessment and Management of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.authors: Teede HJ, Tay CT, Laven JJE, et al.; International PCOS Network
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.finding: Graded recommendations (GRADE strength and certainty) on diagnosis (including AMH), glycaemic assessment, lifestyle, diet, metformin, inositol and ovulation induction with letrozole.
teede-2023-pcos-guideline.limitations: Many recommendations with low or very low certainty; practice points and consensus recommendations carry no certainty rating.
